t: Contraception, emergency contraception and medication abortion
sub: Every method blocks one step between a growing follicle and an implanted embryo, and estrogen, not progestin, carries most of the serious risk.

pretest.q: A woman cannot safely take estrogen. Which kind of hormonal contraception can she still use?
pretest.why: The progestin blocks the LH surge, thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium on its own, so the minipill, the DMPA injection, the implant and the levonorgestrel IUD all work without estrogen.

w.A combined oral pill: Combined pills contain ethinyl estradiol, which raises hepatic clotting factors, so they carry exactly the risk she must avoid.
w.The transdermal patch: The patch delivers ethinyl estradiol through the skin and gives even higher estrogen exposure than most pills, so clot risk is not reduced.
w.The vaginal ring: The ring releases ethinyl estradiol with etonogestrel, so it shares every estrogen contraindication with the pill and the patch.

pretest.q: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception mainly works by which action?
pretest.why: A single high dose of levonorgestrel postpones the LH surge, so the follicle does not rupture while sperm are still alive. It has no effect once a pregnancy has implanted, so it is not an abortifacient.

w.Blocking implantation: Implantation happens about a week after ovulation, and good evidence shows levonorgestrel does not stop an embryo from attaching.
w.Ending an early pregnancy: Ending an implanted pregnancy requires mifepristone and misoprostol; levonorgestrel given after implantation leaves the pregnancy intact.
w.Killing sperm in the uterus: Toxicity to sperm and ova is how the copper IUD works; levonorgestrel acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary instead.

pretest.q: Which drug is given first in a medication abortion?
pretest.why: Mifepristone blocks progesterone receptors, so the decidua breaks down and the uterus becomes sensitive to prostaglandins. Misoprostol follows 24 to 48 hours later to contract the uterus and expel the tissue.

w.Misoprostol: Misoprostol is the second drug; it works far better once mifepristone has withdrawn progesterone support and primed the myometrium.
w.Methotrexate: Methotrexate kills rapidly dividing trophoblast and is the medical treatment for a small ectopic pregnancy, not the standard first drug.
w.Oxytocin: Oxytocin receptors are scarce in the early pregnant uterus, so oxytocin is used for labor and postpartum bleeding instead.

body: How do estrogen and progestin each prevent pregnancy?

Hormonal contraception borrows the ovary's own brake. A steady dose of hormone keeps negative feedback switched on at the hypothalamus and pituitary, so GnRH pulses slow and FSH and LH stay low. The two hormones in {{rp10_chc|combined hormonal contraception}} then split the work. Estrogen blunts FSH, so no follicle becomes dominant, and it steadies the endometrium for predictable bleeding. The progestin blocks the **LH surge**, so ovulation does not happen. It also thickens **cervical mucus**, so sperm cannot swim through, and it thins the endometrium. Because the progestin does most of the contraceptive work, a method can drop estrogen and still prevent pregnancy. It only loses a regular bleeding pattern.
Suppresses FSH, so no follicle becomes dominant
Stabilizes the endometrium; raises SHBG, so free testosterone and acne fall
Venous and arterial clots, because the liver makes more clotting factors
Blocks the LH surge and thickens cervical mucus
Thins the endometrium; irregular spotting when used alone
Bone loss with DMPA; hyperkalemia with drospirenone
Every hormonal method contains a progestin

The progestin reliably stops ovulation and blocks sperm, so every hormonal method has one. Estrogen is added for **cycle control**, and it is the source of the clotting risk. When estrogen is unsafe, the answer is a progestin-only or nonhormonal method, never no contraception.
Which methods contain estrogen, and which work best in real life?

Methods fall into three families. The pill, the weekly **transdermal patch** (with norelgestromin) and the monthly **vaginal ring** (with etonogestrel) all combine ethinyl estradiol with a progestin. The progestin-only family is the minipill, the DMPA injection, the etonogestrel implant and the levonorgestrel IUD. The copper IUD, condoms, the diaphragm and sterilization use no hormone.

Effectiveness depends less on the molecule than on how much the method relies on the user. With {{rp10_typical|typical use}}, about 7 in 100 pill, patch or ring users become pregnant each year, mostly from missed doses. Fewer than 1 in 100 implant or IUD users do. That gap is the cost of user dependence, so {{rp10_larc|long-acting reversible contraception}} is offered first to anyone who wants it, adolescents included.
The only method that also lowers infection risk; latex allergy calls for polyurethane
A fitted dome covers the cervix and holds spermicide
More urinary tract infections; toxic shock syndrome if left in too long
Occluding or removing the fallopian tubes keeps egg and sperm apart
Permanent; when it fails, the pregnancy is more often ectopic
Cutting the vas deferens keeps sperm out of the ejaculate; semen volume is unchanged
Needs a semen analysis to confirm no sperm; permanent

Estrogen raises the liver's output of clotting factors. So every estrogen-containing method raises the risk of **venous thromboembolism** and, in susceptible women, of stroke and myocardial infarction. The contraindications follow from that. They include a smoker over 35, **migraine with aura**, prior VTE or stroke, known thrombophilia, ischemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, fewer than 21 days postpartum, and liver disease such as hepatic adenoma. Current breast cancer, an estrogen-dependent cancer, rules out every hormonal method.

The same pills bring real benefits: lighter, regular, less painful periods, less acne and hirsutism, and a lower lifetime risk of ovarian cancer and endometrial cancer. The same hormones also treat dysmenorrhea, heavy menstrual bleeding and endometriosis.
Rifampin defeats the pill; amoxicillin does not

Only drugs that induce hepatic CYP3A4 lower contraceptive hormone levels: **rifampin**, carbamazepine, phenytoin, topiramate and St John's wort. Ordinary antibiotics such as amoxicillin do not. A woman who must take an {{rp10_inducer|enzyme inducer}} is steered to DMPA, whose high dose outlasts faster metabolism, or to an IUD, which acts locally.
Why do combined pills lower the risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer?

Each ovulation tears the ovarian surface and the nearby tubal epithelium, and every repair is a chance for a mutation. Combined pills suppress ovulation, so ovarian cancer risk falls by about a third, and the protection lasts for decades after stopping. Endometrial cancer is driven by estrogen acting without progesterone. Every active pill contains a progestin, which keeps the lining thin and secretory. The endometrium therefore never sees **unopposed estrogen**, and its cancer risk falls by a similar amount.

{{rp10_btb|Breakthrough bleeding}}, unscheduled bleeding or spotting during active hormone use, is the most common adverse effect of every hormonal method. The pill, patch and ring are used for about 3 weeks, followed by a hormone-free week that causes a planned withdrawal bleed. Breakthrough bleeding is most frequent in the first 3 months, while the endometrium adapts, and it settles in most users. Estrogen stabilizes the lining, so progestin-only and low-dose methods bleed more, as do missed pills, smoking and enzyme inducers. Bleeding that persists prompts a pregnancy test and a check for infection or a polyp before the method is changed. Other effects are nausea, breast tenderness and headache with estrogen, and mood change and acne with progestin.
How do progestin-only methods and IUDs differ?

Progestin-only methods avoid estrogen's clot risk, so they suit women with estrogen contraindications and women who are breastfeeding, but they trade away predictable bleeding. The minipill relies mostly on cervical mucus, so it must be taken at the same time each day. Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (**DMPA**), injected every 3 months, suppresses ovulation so strongly that estradiol stays low. That explains its amenorrhea, bone density loss and slow return of fertility. The etonogestrel **implant**, a rod under the skin of the arm, is the most effective reversible method but causes unpredictable spotting. The **levonorgestrel** IUD thins the endometrium from inside the uterus, so periods lighten or stop, which makes it a first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding. Its effect is mostly local, so ovulation often continues.

The copper IUD contains no hormone. Copper ions cause a sterile inflammatory reaction in the uterus that is toxic to sperm and ova, so fertilization rarely happens. It works for 10 years or more, but periods often become heavier and more painful. Any IUD insertion carries a small risk of **pelvic infection** in the first few weeks, because bacteria from the cervix can be carried upward. Active pelvic inflammatory disease or purulent cervicitis is therefore treated before insertion.
Bone density loss; slow return of fertility
How does emergency contraception differ from medication abortion?

**Emergency contraception** works before implantation, by delaying ovulation or by stopping fertilization. It cannot end a pregnancy that has already implanted, so it is not an **abortifacient**. Levonorgestrel, a single high dose of progestin, works best within 72 hours and only if it is taken before the LH surge begins. It is also less effective as **body mass index** rises, from about 30.

Ulipristal, a {{rp10_sprm|selective progesterone receptor modulator}}, works for up to 5 days. It can still delay follicle rupture after LH has begun to rise, so it beats levonorgestrel late in the window and in obesity. A copper IUD placed within 5 days is the most effective option of all, is not affected by weight, and then keeps working as ongoing contraception.

Medication abortion ends a pregnancy that has already implanted, so its two drugs act after implantation. **Mifepristone** is a progesterone receptor antagonist. Without progesterone's support, the decidua breaks down, the pregnancy detaches, the cervix softens and the myometrium becomes sensitive to prostaglandins. At higher concentrations it also blocks glucocorticoid receptors, so chronic adrenal failure and long-term steroid therapy are contraindications. **Misoprostol**, a prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) analog taken 24 to 48 hours later, drives strong uterine contractions and ripens the cervix to expel the tissue. Misoprostol also protects the stomach lining in NSAID users, but it must be avoided in pregnancy because it causes miscarriage.
The regimen does not treat an ectopic pregnancy, so the location and age of the pregnancy are confirmed first.
It is taken first, so the decidua and cervix are primed before the prostaglandin arrives.
It contracts the myometrium, so cramping and bleeding heavier than a period follow within hours.
A falling hCG or an ultrasound confirms that the pregnancy has passed. Retained tissue is treated with more misoprostol or with uterine aspiration.
How is a method chosen and counseled?

Counseling starts with what the patient wants: when she may want pregnancy, how she feels about bleeding changes, and whether she can use estrogen. Only condoms also prevent sexually transmitted infection. No pelvic examination is needed before starting pills, a patch, a ring, an injection or an implant. An **adolescent** can consent to contraception without a parent in most states. Part of the visit is therefore held alone and kept **confidential**, with the limits of confidentiality explained first. Confidential care makes adolescents more likely to seek care and use contraception, and parental involvement is encouraged but not required.

body.q: A woman had unprotected sex 3 days ago, and a home LH test turned positive yesterday. Which reasoning best explains why levonorgestrel is a poor choice?
o: Levonorgestrel works by blocking implantation, which has already happened three days after intercourse
Levonorgestrel delays ovulation only before the LH surge begins, so once LH is rising it cannot stop follicle rupture
Levonorgestrel would end a pregnancy that has started, so it is avoided after fertilization
Levonorgestrel needs estrogen to suppress FSH, which a single progestin dose cannot do in time
body.why: Levonorgestrel works by postponing the LH surge, so it helps only while the follicle is still waiting for that signal. A positive LH test means the surge has begun, and the follicle will rupture about 36 hours later whatever progestin is given. Implantation comes about a week after ovulation, and levonorgestrel does not disturb it. Ulipristal can still delay rupture after LH starts rising, and a copper IUD blocks fertilization, so either is the better choice.
